requirements.statement: Each image button (<input type="image">) has a text alternative.

citations.quote: Chaque bouton de type `image` (balise `<input>` avec l’attribut `type="image"`) a-t-il une alternative textuelle ?
Vérifier que l’élément `<input>` est pourvu au moins d’une alternative textuelle parmi les suivantes :

routes.statement: A passage of text is associated with the button through aria-labelledby.

citations.quote: Passage de texte associé via l’attribut WAI-ARIA `aria-labelledby` ;

routes.statement: The button's aria-label attribute gives the alternative.
The button's alt attribute gives the alternative.
The button's title attribute gives the alternative.

rationale.text: Unlike the other tests of criterion 1.1, the wording of this one has no qualifier: it asks of every image button whether it has a text alternative, not only of buttons that carry information. Step 2 of the methodology has the auditor decide whether the image carries information, but no step makes the test depend on it: step 3 checks every button against the list and step 4 is the only one that validates. The list is closed: at least one alternative among aria-labelledby, aria-label, alt and title, and the glossary says its order is what constitutes the alternative. So the requirement has four routes. No glossary note sets an exception for an <input>: the notes on images alone in a link or a <button> concern other elements. The candidate is none. The custom check faults an image button when every one of the four sources is absent, empty or only ASCII whitespace, and abstains on a button that is not surely in scope (not exactly type="image", with a role, framed, hidden, not exposed, transparent, outside the viewport or covered), on any non-blank aria-labelledby, on non-blank value text or an associated <label>, and on invisible characters. Its fault is evidence only, because of the browser's fallback name. A native image button with none of the four author sources is not nameless: browsers expose a fallback name for it, a localised default such as Submit (HTML-AAM gives one for an input of type image). The glossary says that where the name computation is only partly supported, the alternative is the value assistive technologies really render, so the fallback may be read as that button's alternative, outside the four listed sources. Whether it counts has not been ruled on. The safeguard Codex proposed, abstaining whenever the browser exposes a fallback name outside the four sources, would leave almost every such button abstained on, since browsers supply the fallback whenever the author gives none; the check would then hardly ever fault. So rather than keep a claim that would almost never fire, the entry is lowered: the link keeps its routes and its whole scope and becomes evidence_only. A fault still shows that no author source exists, which is useful to the auditor, who also judges whether the fallback is relevant. What would raise the entry: a ruling that a fallback name the browser supplies is not an alternative under this test (then the current fault holds), or a check that reads the rendered name with the assistive technologies of the test environment. It is not full in any case: the glossary asks that a title alternative be confirmed with the assistive technologies of the test environment, so the title route could never pass on code alone. axe's input-image-alt examines the four sources but also accepts an implicit or explicit <label>, which the list does not include, so its clean result proves nothing. It skips hidden buttons and those with some explicit roles, so its scope is partial. Its exact handling of hidden and aria-hidden content is not established here, so it is evidence only. Applicability is structural: not applicable follows from the absence of any <input> of type image, which code finds with certainty when every document of the page can be read. Needs is empty: attributes, styles and the accessibility tree are read on the page as loaded.

citations.quote: Si au moins une alternative textuelle est trouvée, **le test est validé**.
Pour chaque élément `<input>` pourvu de l’attribut type="image", déterminer si l’image utilisée est porteuse d’information ;
Cet ordre doit être utilisé pour déterminer ce qui constitue l’alternative textuelle.
c’est la valeur réellement restituée par les technologies d’assistance utilisées dans l’environnement de test (ou « base de référence ») qu’il faudra considérer comme alternative textuelle.
Il faut s’assurer que les assistances techniques présentes dans l’environnement de test retenu restituent correctement l’alternative proposée par l’attribut title.
